headline: Maine algae bloom shifts east as Casco Bay fades and offshore waters intensify
dek: State monitoring finds the inner Casco Bay bloom easing while activity grows from Phippsburg to Port Clyde, with patchy Penobscot Bay blooms and stronger offshore signals.
body: Maine’s latest monitoring bulletin shows a shifting coastal event rather than a bloom that is simply disappearing. The [Maine Department of Marine Resources bulletin](https://www1.maine.gov/dmr/news/wed-09232026-1200-dmr-updates-karenia-mikimotoi-bloom) said Oct. 2 that activity in inner Casco Bay was continuing to dissipate: no significant new water discoloration was reported or observed there that week, cell counts were falling and dissolved oxygen was generally stable despite isolated decreases.

At the same time, the agency said satellite imagery, Marine Patrol flyovers, water samples and fishermen’s observations pointed to increasing activity along the Midcoast, from Phippsburg to Port Clyde. The most active areas were concentrated around peninsulas and ocean-facing embayments. DMR cautioned that the bloom is patchy, so neighboring communities and waterways can experience very different conditions.

The agency also reported patchy Karenia mikimotoi blooms in Penobscot Bay. A DMR sample from Port Clyde exceeded 50 million cells per liter, a level the agency described as a very high-density bloom, although no impacts to marine organisms had been reported there as of the update. Offshore, the bloom had intensified after a recent rain event, with discoloration reported from one-half mile to five miles off the coast between Portland and Penobscot Bay.

DMR is combining satellite information with direct sampling of seawater and marine organisms, dissolved-oxygen measurements and observations from fishermen and Marine Patrol crews. The department said it is working with Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences, the Maine Aquaculture Innovation Center and the University of Maine Darling Center to better understand the event. The agency said chlorophyll-rich areas are presumed to be dominated by Karenia mikimotoi because multiple coastal samples have confirmed the species.

The immediate public-health message is different from the ecological warning. DMR says this species is not a human-health threat and that shellfish and fish harvested from Maine waters remain safe to eat when taken from open areas under the state’s normal harvesting rules. The department’s general biotoxin guidance explains that harvesters must still check current closure notices because other contaminants and toxins can make shellfish unsafe even when water looks clear: [Maine’s shellfish closure notices](https://www.maine.gov/dmr/fisheries/shellfish/closures).

The concern from this bloom is its effect on marine life, especially as dense concentrations decline and decompose. DMR said the most concentrated areas are likely to cause mortality among soft-shell clams and marine worms, while fish and lobsters that can move away from low-oxygen water are less likely to be affected unless they are held in traps or crates. The department said any low-potency toxins produced by Karenia are believed to affect marine organisms through direct contact with their gills, not through the food chain.

That risk has already had economic consequences in Casco Bay. The [Bangor Daily News](https://www.bangordailynews.com/2026/09/22/midcoast/midcoast-environment/maine-algal-bloom-shellfish-die-off/), in a story published through its [Maine Public partnership](https://www.mainepublic.org/climate/2026-09-21/algal-bloom-triggers-emergency-shellfishing-closures), reported emergency harvesting closures in Brunswick and Harpswell after local officials documented severe soft-shell clam losses; Brunswick was Maine’s largest soft-shell clam port in 2025, with nearly $1.8 million in landings. The state’s current update does not establish that the newer Midcoast and Penobscot observations have caused comparable losses.

DMR is asking the public and industry members to report discolored water or marine organisms that are dead or dying to DMRPublicHealthDiv@maine.gov. The department says the appearance may range from rust-colored or brown water to nearly black water, with an odor that can become stronger as a bloom collapses. The agency will continue posting updates as sampling clarifies where the bloom is moving and whether impacts are spreading.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Maine algae bloom shifts east as Casco Bay fades
seoDescription: Maine says the Karenia mikimotoi bloom is easing in inner Casco Bay but increasing along the Midcoast, in Penobscot Bay and offshore.
